materials.heading: Standard materials
materials.lead: The {count} materials in Glazecalc's standard library, from feldspars and clays to frits and boron sources, each with its oxide analysis and its hazards.
materials.intro: Every recipe in Glazecalc can use these materials. Each page gives the oxide analysis and unity contribution Glazecalc works from, the hazards as the library records them, and where the figures come from.
materials.careAbout: Before you handle any glaze material, read <mixing>Safe mixing and ventilation</mixing> and <home>Don't poison your family</home>.
materials.own: Your own materials, saved in your account, are on the <own>Materials page</own>. The <cones>cone chart</cones> lists cone temperatures.

material.lead: A standard material in Glazecalc's library: its oxide analysis, unity contribution and hazards.
material.analysisPercent: Glazecalc has the analysis of {name} as weight percent of the raw material. The unity contribution is the moles of each oxide in the amount of {name} that holds 1.0 mole of flux, which is how Glazecalc adds it into a recipe's unity formula.
material.analysisMolecular: Glazecalc has the analysis of {name} as moles of each fired oxide per formula. The unity contribution is the moles of each oxide in the amount of {name} that holds 1.0 mole of flux, which is how Glazecalc adds it into a recipe's unity formula.
material.noFlux: {name} has no flux oxide, so its unity contribution is per formula as written.
material.weightsNote: The equivalent weight is the grams of {name} that hold 1.0 mole of flux. The fired weight is what is left of that after firing.
material.noAnalysis: Glazecalc could not work out an analysis for this material.
material.noHazards: The library has no hazard statement for this material. Check its safety data sheet from your supplier.
material.care: Glazecalc shows the hazard wording as its record gives it. It is not a full risk assessment, so read the safety data sheet from your supplier. Before you handle any glaze material, read <mixing>Safe mixing and ventilation</mixing> and <home>Don't poison your family</home>.
material.use: Add {name} to a recipe in the Glazecalc calculator to see what it does to a glaze's unity formula.

cones.heading: Cone chart: Orton and SK cones
cones.lead: The temperatures Glazecalc uses for Orton and SK pyrometric cones, in °C and °F, with the heating rate they are for and where each figure comes from.
cones.intro: Cones measure heatwork, which is temperature and time together, not temperature alone. A cone's temperature depends on how fast the kiln heats near the end, so each chart below says its rate. Set a witness cone in the kiln and read it, whatever the chart says. <firing>How to choose, place and read cones</firing> is in the firing guide.
cones.ortonCaption: Orton cones, 022 to 15: large cones heated at {rate} °C an hour ({rateF} °F an hour)
cones.above: Orton also makes cones from 16 to 42. Orton publishes no temperature for them, and no chart we found gives one, so none is shown: {list}.
cones.publishedIntro: Orton's chart of {year} for cones 022 to 14 gives a temperature for each heating rate, over the last 100 °C of the firing. The figures differ a little from the chart above, which Glazecalc uses for cone checks.
cones.publishedCaption: Orton cones, 022 to 14: temperatures in °{unit}, by kind of cone and heating rate
cones.largeDiffers: Large cones 13 and 14 are made differently, with their own temperature equivalents.
cones.skCaption: SK cones, 022 to 20: nominal melt-down temperatures (JIS R 8101)
cones.skIntro: SK (Seger) cones are sold in Japan under the standard {standard}. The figures are the standard's reference temperatures as a seller prints them, not what a kiln will show.
cones.skSource: Source: {seller}, table of standard melt-down temperatures.
